parole.significato: A cauldron of boiling water into which an accused person plunged his forearm, used as a form of trial in Medieval Engla…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin alfetum, from Old English alfæt (“fire-vat”), from āl (“fire”) + fæt (“vat”).

parole.significato: A group of people supporting the same thing or person.
parole.testo: From Latin cohors (stem cohort-); borrowed into Old English as coorta, but reintroduced into Middle English as cōhort and chōors via Old French cohorte. Doublet of court.

parole.significato: A kind of carriage like a gig, originally of wickerwork.
parole.testo: From Old English Crogedene ("saffron valley"), from Old English croh (“saffron”) (< Latin crocus (“saffron”)) + Old English denu (“valley”).

parole.significato: A privilege of setting up, and moving about, sheepfolds, in any fields within manors, in order to manure them or to kee…
parole.testo: From Latin faldagium, from Old English fald (whence English fold). Compare foldage.

parole.significato: To take precedence or superiority over; to preside over.
parole.testo: From fore- (“before”) + sit, sometimes as a calque of Latin praesideō or Old English foresittan.

parole.significato: A member of the Germanic tribe that existed in modern-day Denmark that invaded England about the same time as the Angle…
parole.testo: From Latin plural Iuti, Iutae (in Bede), from Old English Ēotas. Ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *eut, from Proto-Germanic *eutaz, *eutaniz. The spelling was later influenced by Medieval Latin Jutae, Juti.

parole.significato: The periodic discharging of the menses, the flow of blood and cells from the lining of the uterus in unfertilized femal…
parole.testo: From menstruum + -ation, modelled after Late Latin menstruatio. The word is a cognate with French menstruation, Spanish menstruación, which displaced Old English mōnaþblōd (literally “monthblood”).

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Mercia.
parole.testo: From Late Latin Mercius + -an, Latinized from Old English Mierċe.

parole.significato: A requiem mass or other commemoration of a deceased person held one month after burial.
parole.testo: From Middle English monethes mynde under influence from Medieval Latin dies mensis (“day of the month”) and Old English ġemynd, whose principal sense was "memory".
From New Latin ordālium, from Medieval Latin ordālium, from Old English ordāl (“ordeal”), from Proto-West Germanic *uʀdailī. More at ordeal.

parole.testo: From Middle English ordel, ordal, from Medieval Latin ordālium or inherited from its source Old English ordēl, ordāl (“ordeal, judgement”), from Proto-West Germanic *uʀdailī (“judgement”, literally “an out-dealing”), from *uʀdailijan (“to deal out; dispense”). For more, see Old English or-, English
From Medieval Latin portgravius, from Old English portgerēfa &c., from port + gerēfa (“reeve”).
From Latin portgrevius, from Old English portgerēfa, from port + gerēfa (“reeve”).

parole.significato: One of a particular English breed of small sheep with long wool and horns.
parole.testo: From a name of a village in Kent (see Old Romney), from a compound of Latin rumen (“gullet”) and Old English ēa (“river”).

parole.significato: A soc (a medieval right to hold a court or to receive fines).
parole.testo: From Middle English soke, from Medieval Latin (Anglo-Latin) sōca "right of jurisdiction", from Old English sōcn (“jurisdiction, prosecution”, literally “act of seeking”), from Proto-West Germanic *sōkni, from Proto-Germanic *sōkniz (“seeking, inquiry”), from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂g- (“to track”).

parole.testo: From Middle English solar, soler; from a conflation of Old English soler, solere (“raised platform; loft, upper room, upper part of a house, soler”), from Latin sōlārium; and Old English solor, salor (“residence, dwelling; hall; palace”), from Proto-West Germanic *salaʀ, from Proto-Germanic *salaz,

parole.significato: An Anglo-Saxon copper coin of little value, used in Northumbria.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin styca, from Old English stycas, styċġċe pl, Northumbrian variants of Old English styċċe (“small piece of money; bit; piece”).
Perhaps via Medieval Latin *trappa, from Old English træppe /treppe (“trap, snare”), from Proto-Germanic *trap-, from Proto-Indo-European *dreb-, from *der- (“to walk, step”).
